doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

chapter: Learning jazz and finding Latin music
title: Machito, Monterey Jazz Festival and being trans-cultural
summary: As a bike messenger, Machito arranged for him to play Monterey with Dizzy Gillespie in 'Junior's Thing'; Andy Gonzalez later taught him the history of Latin piano; he reflects on not fitting a single category.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I think it’s easier if you’ve grown up with it. I mean invariably, or undoubtedly, not invariably — undoubtedly the sound of Latin music was embedded in my DNA. So on some level subconsciously I did grow up with it. I grew up with Mario Bauza and Machito and people like that were constant visitors to my house. And in fact one of my earliest playing experiences was I was a bicycle messenger and I loved being a bike messenger but it’s a hard gig. And one day it was raining and I must have been about 16 or 17. It was raining. I had hit my knee on the rear view mirror or a side view mirror, and I was just sitting on the side of the sidewalk on the curb kind of just miserable. And Machito walked by. Machito walked by and said, “What are you doing here?” I said, “Machito, this is what I have to do for a living.” And he said to me, “We can’t have this. I’m going to have you — I’m going to commission your father to put on a piece for you, you’re going to conduct it in the Monterey Jazz Festival with Dizzy Gillespie.” And I kind of looked at him going yeah, right, whatever. But it actually happened. He actually got me to play at the Monterey Jazz Festival with Dizzy Gillespie as a guest soloist with the Machito Orchestra in a piece that my father wrote for me that was then entitled “Junior’s Thing” and later became entitled “Pianitis.” But I had the sound of Latin music my entire life. And my entire life I had the sound of that in the back — so when Andy approached me in my 30s to really teach me about Latin music I was ready. I was ready to really sit down and really — because Andy did that. He sat me down and played me the history of Latin piano players. From Bolo Nanyares to Edsel Gomez and everyone in between. And then I realized that this music that I — and this is funny because it begs the question what happens to people who are trans-cultural? The people who are in New York City but can’t identify or be identified as either white or black or Latino enough. I mean and this is really strange.
